title: Enteral Nutrition (Tube Feeding) Administration
summary: Administering tube feeding via nasogastric, nasojejunal, or gastrostomy tube.
steps: Verify tube placement before initiating or resuming feeding: pH <5.5 confirms gastric position (pH 5.5–6 = re-check). Confirm via X-ray if pH is questionable.
Elevate HOB to at least 30–45° during feeding and for 30–60 minutes after (reduces aspiration risk).
Assess gastric residual volume (GRV) per policy (typically q4h for continuous feeds): aspirate via syringe. GRV >500mL = hold feeding and notify provider.
Return aspirated residual unless policy states otherwise (avoids electrolyte loss).
Flush tube with 30mL water before and after feeding/medications (15mL for critically ill/fluid-restricted).
Prime feeding pump tubing. Set rate per order. Connect to feeding port of tube.
Label feeding tubing with date and time — change tubing per policy (q24h).
Assess bowel sounds, abdominal distension, nausea, diarrhea, and stool output each shift.
Monitor blood glucose as ordered (tube feeding can cause hyperglycemia).
Use enteral-only tubing (ENFit connectors) — prevents wrong-route errors with IV tubing.
safetyTips: Confirm tube placement EVERY time before feeding — tube migration can lead to pulmonary aspiration.
ENFit connectors are designed to prevent IV↔enteral wrong-route errors. Never connect IV tubing to a feeding tube.
Aspiration is the most serious complication — HOB elevation and GRV checks are protective.
documentation: Tube placement confirmation method and result

title: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) Administration
summary: Administering TPN safely through a central venous access device with monitoring for metabolic complications.
steps: Verify TPN label matches the MAR: patient name, MRN, formula components, rate, and expiration. Two-nurse check required.
TPN must be administered through a dedicated central line lumen — never through a peripheral IV (osmolarity >900 mOsm/L damages veins).
Use a 1.2-micron in-line filter to trap precipitates.
Inspect the bag: clear solution without cloudiness, precipitate, or discoloration. Do NOT use if lipids are separated (cracked emulsion).
Connect to dedicated central line lumen using aseptic technique. Label as TPN line.
Set rate per order. Do NOT hang TPN with other IV medications (incompatibility risk).
Monitor blood glucose every 4–6 hours initially (goal 140–180 mg/dL in most ICU patients).
Monitor labs: BMP (glucose, electrolytes, BUN/Cr), LFTs, phosphorus, magnesium, triglycerides per schedule.
Refeeding syndrome risk: low phosphorus, potassium, magnesium after initiation in malnourished patients. Start TPN at low rate and advance.
If TPN must be suddenly stopped, hang D10W at the same rate to prevent hypoglycemia.
safetyTips: Never use TPN line for blood draws, blood products, or other medications.
Cracked lipid emulsion (orange streaks, layering) = DO NOT USE. Return to pharmacy.
Refeeding syndrome: check phosphorus, K+, Mg2+ before starting TPN in severely malnourished patients.
keyTakeaways: Monitor glucose q4–6h; D10W if suddenly stopped

title: Intake & Output (I&O) Measurement
summary: Accurately measuring and documenting all fluid intake and output to monitor fluid balance.
steps: INTAKE: Document all fluid inputs every shift and cumulatively every 24 hours.
IV fluids: read infusion pump totals at each shift change.
Oral intake: use patient reporting + estimated volumes from food trays (1oz = 30mL).
Other inputs: blood products, IV medications, tube feeding, irrigation fluids.
OUTPUT: Document all fluid outputs.
Urine: measure in graduated hat (toilet) or catheter bag. Normal: 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr adult.
Emesis: estimate in mL using basin measurements.
Drains: wound drains, NG output, chest tube, colostomy.
Insensible losses (not directly measurable): estimate 500–1000mL/day (respiration + perspiration).
Report: urine output <0.5mL/kg/hr × 2 hours (oliguria). Urine output <30mL/hr = notify provider.
Calculate fluid balance: Total Intake − Total Output = Fluid Balance.
Positive balance (more in than out): edema risk. Negative balance: dehydration risk.
safetyTips: Urine output <30mL/hr for 2 consecutive hours in an adult = notify provider — may indicate AKI or shock.
Never estimate urine without measuring — guessing invalidates the fluid balance and clinical decision-making.
Diuretic administration should be followed by output monitoring to confirm response.
documentation: Urine output per hour if ordered or clinically indicated

title: Hemodialysis Vascular Access Assessment (AV Fistula / Graft)
summary: Assessing and protecting arteriovenous fistulas and grafts used for hemodialysis access.
steps: Assess AV fistula/graft every shift.
AUSCULTATE: Place stethoscope over the access site. A continuous machine-like bruit = patent access. Absence of bruit = possible thrombosis. Report immediately.
PALPATE: Feel for a continuous thrill (vibration) = normal flow. Absence of thrill = possible thrombosis.
Inspect site: redness, warmth, swelling, skin breakdown, signs of infection, aneurysm.
PROTECT THE ACCESS ARM: NO blood pressure measurements, NO blood draws, NO IV insertions on the fistula arm. Post sign at bedside.
No tight clothing, jewelry, or restraints on the fistula arm.
Patient education: no sleeping on fistula arm, avoid lifting heavy objects, check thrill daily.
Post-dialysis: assess needle site for bleeding or hematoma. Apply finger pressure x15 minutes if bleeding.
Notify dialysis team and provider immediately if: bruit/thrill absent, significant swelling, excessive bleeding, signs of infection.
safetyTips: Loss of thrill or bruit = thrombosis until proven otherwise — STAT notification to provider/dialysis team.
Never take BP in the fistula arm — even once. One incorrect measurement can clot the access.
Fistula is the patient's lifeline — treat it with absolute care.
keyTakeaways: No BP/IV/blood draws on fistula arm

title: Nutritional Screening & Assessment
summary: Performing admission nutritional screening and referring at-risk patients to a registered dietitian.
equipment: Nutritional screening tool (MUST, NRS-2002, or facility tool)
steps: Screen all admitted patients within 24 hours using the facility's validated tool.
MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool) — community/hospital:
Step 2: Unintentional weight loss in past 3–6 months (>10%=2, 5–10%=1).
Step 3: Acute disease effect (not eating >5 days = +2).
Score 0=low risk, 1=medium risk, 2+=high risk — refer to dietitian.
Assess: appetite changes, dysphagia, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, recent dietary restrictions.
Assess: muscle wasting (temporal, thenar eminence), edema (can mask weight loss), ascites.
Review labs: albumin, prealbumin, total protein, lymphocyte count, transferrin.
Dysphagia screen (bedside): observe patient drinking small amount of water. Coughing, wet voice, or choking = refer to speech-language pathology.
Refer high-risk patients to registered dietitian within 24–48 hours.
safetyTips: Albumin reflects inflammation and hydration status more than acute nutritional status — prealbumin is a better short-term marker.
Dysphagia increases aspiration risk — do not offer oral diet until cleared by SLP if dysphagia is suspected.
Malnutrition is associated with increased LOS, pressure injuries, infections, and mortality.
keyTakeaways: MUST score ≥2 = high risk, refer dietitian
